title: Linearized gravitational waves and their detection
one_line_summary: Expands the metric to first order about Minkowski space and uses gauge freedom to show that plane gravitational waves are transverse and carry two polarizations (+ and x). It solves the sourced wave equation with the retarded Green's function to reach the quadrupole formula, then works out a circular binary's waveform, Isaacson energy flux, luminosity and period decay, checked against binary pulsars. It explains how test masses, resonant bars, interferometers, radar timing, Doppler tracking and pulsar timing arrays respond to a passing wave, and closes with a survey of sources and the LIGO/Virgo detections.
role_in_book: First chapter of Part E (Gravitational Waves), placed after the black-hole chapters. It turns the book's earlier machinery on the weak-field, radiative regime: tensor calculus and geodesic coordinates (Ch. 6), geodesic deviation (Ch. 10), the Lagrangian field-equation method (Ch. 11), Maxwell potentials and gauge (Ch. 12), Kepler motion (Ch. 16) and Bondi's radar k-calculus (Ch. 2). The perturbative picture built here (transverse waves, two polarizations, quadrupole emission, energy defined only as an average) is the baseline that Ch. 22 compares with exact plane waves and Ch. 23 replaces with Bondi's nonlinear treatment of radiation and mass loss. It is also the book's main link between theory and present-day observation: binary pulsars, LIGO/Virgo and LISA.

assumed_background.topic: Component calculus of Christoffel symbols and the Riemann, Ricci and Einstein tensors; the Riemann symmetries and cyclic identity
Geodesic (locally inertial) coordinates in which first derivatives of the metric vanish at a point
Tensor transformation law for the metric under a change of coordinates, eq. (7.5)
Einstein field equations with coupling constant kappa, and the equation of geodesic deviation in tetrad form, eqs (10.21), (10.37)
Obtaining field equations from a Lagrangian density by Euler-Lagrange variation
Energy-momentum tensor, its conservation, and Maxwell's equations in potential form with gauge transformations and the Lorenz condition; the d'Alembertian (12.40)
Bondi k-calculus: measuring distance with radar pulses and the constancy of light speed
Classical Kepler motion and why orbits lie in a plane
Weak-field Schwarzschild metric in isotropic coordinates (used in Exercise 21.5)
Two-body problem: centre of mass, reduced mass, Lagrangian mechanics in polar coordinates
Driven damped harmonic oscillator and resonance amplitude
Divergence theorem, integration by parts in three dimensions, spherical polar volume integrals
Dirac delta function, d'Alembert's solution of the 1D wave equation, Green's function method for PDEs
Michelson interferometer, optical path difference and interference fringes
Pulsars, neutron stars, compact binaries and black holes as astrophysical objects

learning_objectives: Reader can expand g_ab = eta_ab + epsilon h_ab to first order and write the linearized Christoffel symbols, Riemann tensor, Ricci tensor and Einstein tensor in terms of h_ab.
Reader can derive how h_ab changes under an infinitesimal coordinate shift x^a -> x^a + epsilon xi^a and show that the linearized Riemann tensor is unchanged.

Reader can introduce the trace-reversed perturbation, impose the Lorentz (harmonic, de Donder) gauge by solving a wave equation for xi_a, and reduce the linearized field equations to a sourced wave equation, identifying the residual gauge freedom.
Reader can explain why a wave equation for h_ab alone does not establish that gravity propagates, whereas a wave equation for the Riemann tensor does, and why energy transport is a further question.
Reader can reduce a plane-wave perturbation h_ab(t - x) to transverse-traceless canonical form with only two free functions and state the physical content of the + and x polarizations.
Reader can predict the deformation of a ring of free particles by + and x waves, including the 45-degree relation between the two polarizations and the absence of longitudinal motion.
Reader can build the retarded solution of the sourced wave equation from a point-source fundamental solution and apply the far-zone and long-wavelength approximations.

Reader can derive the quadrupole formula Phi_ij = -(2/r) d^2 I_ij/dt^2 (t - r) from energy-momentum conservation, and evaluate it for an equal-mass circular binary, getting frequency 2 Omega and amplitude 8 Omega^2 m R^2 / r.

Reader can explain why gravitational energy cannot be a local tensor density, define the Isaacson tensor as a wavelength-averaged second-order effective stress-energy, and compute the flux (A_+^2 + A_x^2) omega^2 / 32 pi of a monochromatic wave.

Reader can obtain the angular pattern and total luminosity 128/5 m^2 R^4 Omega^6 of an equal-mass circular binary, both by TT projection plus angular integration and from the reduced-quadrupole formula, and use energy balance to predict orbital period decay scaling as T^(-5/3).
Reader can show that free test masses keep fixed TT coordinates while their proper separation oscillates, and reproduce that result with geodesic deviation and with radar return times.

Reader can estimate interferometer arm-length changes and fringe shifts, model a resonant bar as a driven oscillator, and explain when the short-detector approximation fails (LISA, pulsar timing, Doppler tracking).

Reader can classify gravitational-wave sources (burst, periodic, stochastic) and describe how matched filtering, two-site timing and multi-detector triangulation turned GW150914, GW170814 and GW170817 into confident detections with measured source parameters.

teaching_approach.summary: The chapter is a long derivation ladder that runs alongside electromagnetism. Each linearized-gravity step has a Maxwell counterpart (gauge transformation, Lorenz gauge, sourced wave equation, retarded potential, polarization), and the authors then point out where gravity goes further: polarizations 45 degrees apart and an energy with no local density. The treatment is explicitly component-based. Plane-wave Riemann components are listed in groups, gauge conditions are integrated by hand, and the binary luminosity is derived twice by independent routes. Physical meaning is taken from invariant measurements (proper distance, geodesic deviation, radar return time), and the chapter shows these agree with one another. The last third becomes an observational survey: numbers, reproduced data plots, detector designs and detection history up to about 2020.
narrative_arc: Assume a small perturbation of flat spacetime with asymptotic flatness and linearize every curvature quantity; note the Lagrangian that generates the linear Einstein tensor.
Treat infinitesimal coordinate changes as gauge transformations of h_ab, by analogy with electromagnetic potentials; show that curvature is gauge invariant.
Trace-reverse the perturbation, impose the Lorentz gauge by solving a wave equation for the gauge vector, and obtain a sourced wave equation plus leftover gauge freedom.
Ask whether waves really exist: reject the gauge-dependent argument from h_ab and use the wave equation satisfied by the Riemann tensor, while noting that energy transport is still unproven.

Take a plane-wave ansatz, list the Riemann components, apply the vacuum equations to isolate the physical components h22, h23, h33, then use gauge conditions, boundary conditions and residual gauge freedom to reach the two-function canonical (TT) form.
Give the two functions physical meaning through the proper distance between free particles: + polarization, then x polarization as a 45-degree rotated copy.
Turn to sources: solve the wave equation with a point source, normalize by integrating over a ball, superpose to get the retarded integral, then use far-zone and long-wavelength approximations.
Use energy-momentum conservation to trade the stress integral for the second time derivative of the mass moment: the quadrupole formula.
Apply it to an equal-mass Newtonian circular binary: Kepler relation, mass moments, a waveform at twice the orbital frequency; caveat about self-gravitating sources.

Face the energy problem: equivalence principle and lack of background symmetry forbid a local energy density; build the second-order effective stress tensor, average it over wavelengths to get the gauge-invariant Isaacson tensor, and compute the flux of a monochromatic wave.
Compute the binary's flux in an arbitrary direction by rotating and TT-projecting, integrate over the sphere to get total power, and confirm it with the reduced-quadrupole formula.
Balance radiated power against Newtonian orbital energy to get period decay and compare with the Hulse-Taylor and double-pulsar data.
Return to measurement: free particles sit at fixed TT coordinates; proper distance, geodesic deviation and a spring-mass bar model all show the tidal strain.

Model a Michelson interferometer, estimate the tiny fringe shift, and redo the measurement properly with radar timing along null geodesics, valid even when the detector is not small compared with the wavelength.

Survey detector types (bars, ground interferometers, LISA, Doppler tracking, pulsar timing arrays), source classes, sensitivity curves, and the LIGO/Virgo detections with matched filtering and sky localization.
signature_moves: Electromagnetic shadowing: gauge transformations, the Lorentz gauge and polarization are introduced by explicit analogy with the Maxwell potential A_a, and the analogy's breaking points (45 degrees vs 90 degrees, no local energy) are stated.
Gauge-invariant existence argument: wave propagation is established through the box operator acting on R_abcd rather than on h_ab.
Group-by-group listing of all twenty Riemann components of a plane wave, so the vacuum equations visibly kill the unphysical block and leave h22, h23, h33.
Obtaining the x polarization from the + polarization by an explicit 45-degree rotation of the line element, rather than by solving the problem again.

Normalizing the retarded point-source solution by integrating the wave equation over a small ball (divergence theorem plus a radial integration by parts), avoiding Green's-function theory until the result is in hand.
Deriving the quadrupole formula from the double divergence of the stress tensor integrated against x^l x^m, so that conservation does the physics.
Two independent computations of the binary luminosity (angular TT projection and integration vs reduced-quadrupole formula), both giving 128/5.
Three independent readouts of the same tidal strain (metric proper distance, geodesic deviation, radar return time), each shown to agree to first order.
Reusing the Chapter 2 radar method in curved spacetime (Synge's differential chronometry) to make detector response a timing calculation.

sections.title: The linearized field equations
sections.summary: Sets up weak-field gravity as a small perturbation of Minkowski space in Minkowski coordinates, keeping only first order in a bookkeeping parameter epsilon and requiring the perturbation to vanish at large radius. The inverse metric, Christoffel symbols, Riemann tensor, Ricci tensor, Ricci scalar and Einstein tensor are all written in terms of h_ab and its trace, with indices moved by eta. The authors warn that recasting GR as a Lorentz-covariant field theory has limits, especially for gravitational energy, and note that the linear Einstein tensor follows from a quadratic Lagrangian in derivatives of h.
key_moves: Write g_ab = eta_ab + epsilon h_ab and guess the inverse g^ab = eta^ab - epsilon h^ab by checking the product equals delta to first order.
Because Christoffel symbols are already order epsilon, indices on h may be raised and lowered with eta alone.
Linear Riemann tensor contains only second derivatives of h; the Bianchi identities are satisfied identically.
Contract to Ricci and Einstein tensors, introducing the trace h and the box operator.
Show that G_ab is minus the divergence of the derivative of a quadratic Lagrangian with respect to h^ab_,c.

sections.title: Gauge transformations
sections.summary: An infinitesimal coordinate change shifts h_ab by the symmetrized derivative of a vector, which the authors call a gauge transformation by analogy with electromagnetism; curvature is unchanged by it. Trace-reversing h_ab to phi_ab simplifies the Einstein tensor, and imposing zero divergence of phi_ab (Lorentz, de Donder or harmonic gauge) turns the field equations into a wave equation with the stress tensor as source. Reaching the gauge means solving a sourced wave equation for xi_a; any further xi_a satisfying the source-free wave equation preserves the gauge. In vacuum both phi_ab and h_ab satisfy the homogeneous wave equation.
concepts: gauge transformation of the metric perturbation
linearized field equations as wave equations
key_moves: Apply the metric transformation law to x' = x + epsilon xi to get h' = h - 2 xi_(a,b).
Rewrite Ricci and Einstein tensors in terms of phi_ab = h_ab - (1/2) eta_ab h.
Observe that the divergence terms disappear if phi^a_b,a = 0.
Compute how the divergence of phi changes under a gauge shift: it drops by box xi_b, so choosing box xi_b equal to the old divergence reaches the gauge.
Field equations become (1/2) epsilon box phi_ab = -kappa T_ab; in vacuum the trace of the equation shows box h = 0, hence box h_ab = 0.
Note that xi with box xi = 0 remains available.

sections.title: Linearized plane gravitational waves
sections.summary: First asks what really shows that gravitational effects propagate. A wave equation for h_ab is gauge dependent, but it implies a wave equation for the gauge-invariant Riemann tensor, so curvature travels at light speed (whether energy is carried is left for later). Assuming h depends only on t and x, the Riemann components split into a vanishing group, a group that vacuum equations force to zero, and a group built only from h22, h23, h33. Sharpening the ansatz to h(t - x), the Lorentz gauge conditions are integrated and the integration functions set to zero by asymptotic flatness, and residual gauge vectors of the form F(t - x) remove h00, h02, h03 and h11. The result is a canonical transverse-traceless matrix with only h22 = -h33 and h23 nonzero.
concepts: wave equation for the Riemann tensor
key_moves: Box R_abcd = 0 follows from box h_ab = 0, giving a gauge-invariant propagation statement.
Plane symmetry (no y, z dependence) makes the Riemann tensor degenerate: three groups (21.38)-(21.40).
Vacuum Ricci equations, e.g. R_13 = R_0103 = 0, force the whole mixed group (21.39) to vanish, leaving only components from h22, h23, h33.
Split h into a transverse block and a remainder whose curvature vanishes, suggesting the remainder is pure gauge.
Integrate Lorentz gauge conditions for h(t - x); boundary conditions set the integration functions to zero, giving h33 = -h22 and linking other components.
Choose residual gauge functions F_a(u) with dF/du fixed by h00, h11, h02, h03 to eliminate those components, reaching (21.54).

sections.title: Polarization states of plane waves
sections.summary: Interprets the two remaining functions through proper distance. For an h22-wave the proper separation of neighbouring free particles along y is scaled by (1 - epsilon h22) and along z by (1 + epsilon h22), while separations along the propagation direction are unaffected, so a ring of dust in the transverse plane pulses into ellipses alternately elongated along y and z: the + polarization. An h23-wave becomes identical to an h22-wave after a 45-degree rotation of the transverse axes, giving the x polarization. A general wave superposes the two, and their 45-degree relative orientation (versus 90 degrees for light) is traced to gravity being a symmetric rank-2 tensor field.
concepts: proper distance in a gravitational-wave spacetime
key_moves: Write the line element for an h22-wave and compute proper separations along y and along z separately.
Since proper distance is coordinate independent, opposite-sign changes along y and z mean real physical squeezing and stretching.
Separation along x is unchanged, so the effect is purely transverse.
Rotate y, z by 45 degrees to convert the off-diagonal h23 term into the diagonal h22 form.
Contrast the 45-degree separation of polarizations with the 90-degree separation for electromagnetic waves.

sections.title: Solving the wave equation
sections.summary: Absorbs epsilon into Phi_ab and treats each component as a scalar wave equation with source -2 kappa T_ab. For a point source at the origin with time-dependent strength q(t), spherical symmetry reduces the problem away from the origin to a 1D wave equation for r phi, whose outgoing (causal) solution is u(t - r)/r. Integrating the equation over a small ball fixes 4 pi u = q. Taking q as a delta function gives the fundamental solution, and superposing shifted copies gives the retarded-time integral. For a compact source observed far away with wavelength much longer than the source, the retarded time is approximately t - r everywhere in the source, and the perturbation is -4/r times the volume integral of T_ab at retarded time (geometric units).
concepts: fundamental solution of the wave equation
key_moves: Use the radial Laplacian identity to turn the 3D radial wave equation into a 1D one for psi = r phi.
Apply d'Alembert's general solution and discard the incoming part on causal grounds.
Integrate over a ball of radius a: the Laplacian term via the divergence theorem, the time-derivative term by radial integration by parts; the a-dependent terms cancel, leaving 4 pi u(t) = q(t).
Move the delta source to (s, y) and superpose using the sifting property; the time delta sets s to the retarded time.
For r >> R_0 and lambda >> R_0 replace |x - y| by r in both the denominator and the phase, making the result the total source integral at t - r divided by 4 pi r.

sections.title: The quadrupole formula
sections.summary: Relates the far field directly to the source's motion. Linearized conservation of T^ab gives the second time derivative of T^00 as the double spatial divergence of T^jk. Multiplying by x^l x^m and integrating by parts twice, with no boundary terms for a compact source, shows the volume integral of T^ij is half the second time derivative of the second mass moment. Inserting this into the far-zone solution gives the quadrupole formula: the spatial perturbation equals -2/r times the second time derivative of I_ij evaluated at retarded time.
concepts: quadrupole formula for the wave field
key_moves: Take the time component of the conservation law, differentiate in time, and substitute the spatial components of the law to reach a double divergence.
Integrate x^l x^m times the double divergence by parts twice; derivatives of x^l x^m produce Kronecker deltas and a factor 2.
Identify T^00 with mass-energy density mu and define I^ij = integral of y^i y^j mu.
Substitute into (21.87) to get Phi_ij = -(2/r) second time derivative of I_ij at t - r.

sections.title: The quadrupole generated by a binary star system
sections.summary: Models a binary with Newtonian mechanics: the two-body Lagrangian separates into free centre-of-mass motion and a reduced-mass particle in an inverse-square potential. For equal masses m on a circle of radius R about the centre of mass, Omega^2 = m/(4R^3) (G = 1). Writing the density as a pair of delta functions gives mass moments oscillating at 2 Omega, and the quadrupole formula yields a field whose only nonzero components lie in the orbital-plane (xy) block, of + and x type as seen along the orbital axis, with amplitude 8 m Omega^2 R^2 / r at frequency 2 Omega. The authors caution that flat-space conservation does not strictly hold for a self-gravitating source, but cite the result that Newtonian source motion plus the far-zone quadrupole formula is adequate.
concepts: Kepler's third law for a circular binary
frequency doubling of binary gravitational waves
quadrupole formula for the wave field
key_moves: Change variables to centre of mass and relative separation; centre of mass moves freely and is placed at the origin.
Circular orbit: angular momentum conservation gives constant Omega; radial Euler-Lagrange equation gives Omega^2 = 2m/a^3 with a = 2R.
Delta-function density for two point stars at opposite positions.
Moments I_xx, I_yy, I_xy contain cos 2 Omega t and sin 2 Omega t via double-angle identities.
Two time derivatives give the factor 4 Omega^2 and the waveform (21.108).
Caveat: near-zone motion needs the covariant conservation law, but Newtonian motion suffices for the far-zone estimate.

sections.title: Gravitational energy
sections.summary: Explains why gravitational-wave energy is subtle. First, the equivalence principle lets metric derivatives vanish at any point, so no tensorial local energy density quadratic in them can exist. Second, conserved energy normally comes from background symmetries, and GR has no fixed background. Around flat space these problems can be managed by averaging over several wavelengths. A heuristic argument gives a flux proportional to amplitude squared times frequency squared, with coefficient 1/32 pi. The careful version expands the metric to second order: the second-order part of the Ricci tensor, built from the first-order wave, acts as a source for the second-order metric and defines an effective stress tensor t_ab. That tensor is not gauge invariant pointwise, but its spacetime average (the Isaacson tensor) is. In TT gauge only one term survives, and a monochromatic wave has energy density and flux (h_+^2 + h_x^2) omega^2 / 32 pi.
concepts: effective energy-momentum tensor of gravitational waves
key_moves: Equivalence-principle argument: derivatives of g vanish in geodesic coordinates, so a local energy density built from them cannot be a tensor.
Symmetry argument: no fixed background, so Noether-type conservation is unavailable in general; flat background is invariantly defined by zero curvature.
Heuristic: Lagrangian quadratic in derivatives, so energy flux is proportional to A^2 omega^2 cos^2, which averages to one half.
Expand to epsilon^2; vacuum equations give R^(1)(h^(2)) + R^(2)(h^(1)) = 0; move the quadratic part to the right as 8 pi t_ab.
Average over a region several wavelengths across; total divergences drop out, so derivatives can be moved between factors.
Show the averaged tensor is unchanged by gauge shifts; in TT gauge it reduces to (1/32 pi) average of h_cd,a h^cd_,b.
Evaluate for a monochromatic x-polarized wave along z, then add the + polarization.

sections.title: Gravitational energy-flux from a binary system
sections.summary: Applies the flux formula to the binary. Along the orbital axis the field is already TT, with two polarizations of amplitude 8 Omega^2 m R^2 / r at 2 Omega, giving power per solid angle (16/pi)(Omega^3 m R^2)^2. For a direction at angle theta from the axis, the field is rotated into a frame whose third axis is that direction, projected transverse and made traceless, giving A_+ proportional to (1 + cos^2 theta) and A_x proportional to 2 cos theta. The resulting pattern (cos^4 + 6 cos^2 + 1) is integrated over the sphere to give total power 128/5 m^2 R^4 Omega^6, rewritten in terms of the period. The general reduced-quadrupole formula (1/5)<third derivative of the traceless quadrupole squared> is quoted (derived in exercises) and checked against the binary result.
concepts: angular distribution of binary gravitational radiation
key_moves: Luminosity per solid angle = flux times r^2; along z both polarizations contribute equally.
Rotate the spatial tensor with a rotation matrix about the y-axis by theta.
TT-project: keep the transverse 2x2 block and subtract half its trace from the diagonal.
Read off A_+ and A_x, sum squares, integrate (cos^4 + 6 cos^2 + 1) sin theta over the sphere: 32/5 times 2 pi.
Cross-check via the reduced quadrupole: third time derivative has magnitude 8 m R^2 Omega^3, contraction gives 128 m^2 R^4 Omega^6, divide by 5.

sections.title: Effects of gravitational radiation on the orbit of a binary system
sections.summary: Writes the Newtonian energy of the equal-mass circular binary as -(m/4)(4 pi m / T)^(2/3), negative because of the potential energy, and sets its rate of change equal to minus the radiated power. This gives a period derivative whose magnitude scales as T^(-5/3), testable by long-term pulsar timing. The Hulse-Taylor discovery (1974, Arecibo) and its parameters are described, along with the 2003 double pulsar. Reproduced plots show cumulative periastron-time shifts following the GR curve.
concepts: binding energy of a circular binary
key_moves: Express kinetic plus potential energy in terms of R, then in terms of T via Kepler.
Differentiate with respect to time to link dE/dt to dT/dt.
Impose energy balance with the radiated power (with a minus sign) and solve for dT/dt.
Compare with pulsar timing data: cumulative periastron shift grows quadratically in time.

sections.title: Measuring gravitational wave displacements
sections.summary: Detectors monitor free test masses. For a particle initially at rest in a TT-gauge wave, the geodesic equation to first order involves only Gamma^a_00, which vanishes, so the particle stays at fixed TT coordinates and TT time is its proper time. The proper separation of two such particles nevertheless oscillates as (1 - epsilon h22/2) L. Geodesic deviation in an adapted tetrad, which uses the gauge-invariant Riemann tensor, gives the same result. The section then discusses Weber's resonant bars and the controversy over their claims, models a bar as two masses on a damped spring driven by the wave, and derives the resonant amplification. It then describes an L-shaped Michelson interferometer with suspended test masses, computes the arm-length difference A L sin(omega t), estimates a fringe shift of order 10^-12 for a 1 km arm, explains the need for Fabry-Perot cavities, and notes that proper distance is not quite what light measures when arms are not small compared with the wavelength.
concepts: geodesic motion of test masses in a gravitational wave
proper distance in a gravitational-wave spacetime
key_moves: Perturb the 4-velocity about (1,0,0,0); the first-order geodesic equation reduces to dV/dtau = -Gamma^a_00 = 0 for the TT metric.
Integrate the proper length along y at fixed t: (1 - epsilon h22)^(1/2) L, approximately (1 - epsilon h22 / 2) L.
Write geodesic deviation with R^alpha_0beta0, insert plane-wave Riemann components, and integrate to first order.
Replace the spring's coordinate extension by its proper extension to obtain a forcing term (1/2) L times the second derivative of h22.
Steady-state resonance amplitude grows as the damping decreases.
Arm lengths change by -/+ (1/2) A L sin(omega t); the difference A L sin(omega t) sets the phase shift.
Numerical estimate: A ~ 10^-21, L = 1 km gives Delta L ~ 10^-18 m, about 10^-12 of an infrared wavelength.

Straight lines extremize flat-space length, so path corrections are second order; the first-order change comes from the metric along the straight path, valid when the arm is much shorter than the wavelength.

sections.title: A direct interferometric measurement
sections.summary: Recasts detection in the spirit of the k-calculus: a freely falling observer times radar echoes from a distant free mass, and many such measurements determine spacetime geometry (Synge's differential chronometry). In a TT h22-wave travelling along z, the outgoing and returning null rays along x are integrated to first order, treating the unperturbed path as a straight line. The return time is 2L plus two integrals of h22 sampled along the flat light path. For a detector small compared with the wavelength this reduces to a delay -epsilon L h22, consistent with proper distance. Differentiating with respect to emission time gives dT/dt = 1 - (epsilon/2)[h22(t + 2L) - h22(t)], which depends only on the wave at emission and at echo return and is the form needed for large detectors. Expanding for small L and differentiating again recovers the geodesic-deviation result.
concepts: round-trip light travel time in a gravitational wave
detector response beyond the long-wavelength limit
key_moves: Null condition along x: (dt/dx)^2 = 1 - epsilon h22, so dt/dx is approximately 1 - epsilon h22 / 2.
Evaluate h22 along the unperturbed ray t = t0 + x, since corrections are second order.
Do the same for the return leg, changing variables to x-tilde = L - x.
Small-detector limit: both integrands approximately h22(t0), so the round-trip delay is -epsilon L h22.
Differentiate the exact first-order T with respect to t0; the integrals of derivatives telescope into endpoint values.
Taylor-expand h22(t + 2L) to recover dT/dt = 1 - epsilon L dh22/dt, and the second derivative matches geodesic deviation.

sections.title: The detection of gravitational waves
sections.summary: Surveys four detector concepts. Cryogenic resonant bars (sensitivity around h ~ 10^-20, narrow band, no confirmed detections; spherical versions proposed). Ground interferometers operating from about 20 Hz to 2 kHz: the two LIGO sites, Virgo, GEO600, with best strain sensitivity near 10^-23 per root hertz. The space interferometer LISA: three spacecraft in a triangle trailing Earth by about 20 degrees, sensitive around 10^5 times lower frequency, needing the general timing formula with an angle-dependent response (21.179). Doppler tracking of interplanetary spacecraft, where a burst imprints three times on the round-trip signal, with sensitivity about 10^-13 to 10^-15. Pulsar timing arrays, where correlated Earth-term delays across several millisecond pulsars can reveal waves with periods of years.
concepts: detector response beyond the long-wavelength limit
key_moves: Match detector size to wavelength: ground detectors are small enough for (21.174); LISA above about 10 mHz is not.
Oblique incidence modifies the timing response with sin theta weighted terms, including a mid-path sample (exercise 21.21).
Doppler tracking and pulsar timing are direct uses of the timing formulas (21.173) and (21.172), limited by clock stability.
Multiple pulsars share the Earth-end perturbation, which provides a correlation signature.

sections.title: Sources of gravitational radiation and the observation of gravitational waves
sections.summary: Classifies sources as bursts (compact-binary mergers, extreme-mass-ratio inspirals, supermassive black-hole mergers), periodic (binaries, spinning neutron stars, pulsating white dwarfs) and stochastic (primordial background, unresolved binaries). Notes that numerical relativity is needed for strong-field estimates and presents strain/sensitivity plots. It then narrates the LIGO programme: initial design sensitivity by 2005, the S6 run, the Advanced LIGO upgrade, and the first detection GW150914 (chirp at 35-250 Hz, 7 ms inter-site delay, 5.1 sigma, about 35 + 30 solar masses forming a 62 solar-mass Kerr hole with spin about 0.68, three solar masses radiated). It explains matched filtering against template banks built from post-Newtonian inspiral, numerical-relativity merger and quasinormal-mode ringdown, why a detector network is needed for sky localization (GW170814), and summarizes early catalogue events including GW170729, GW170818 and the multi-messenger neutron-star merger GW170817.
concepts: sky localization by a detector network
key_moves: Distinguish instantaneous strain from characteristic strain accumulated over an observation time when reading sensitivity plots.
Two-site coincidence window is bounded by light travel time between detectors.
Template matching yields distance (from amplitude) and masses (from frequency evolution).
Kepler plus GW frequency: 75 Hz orbital frequency implies about 350 km separation at merger.
Arrival-time triangulation across three or more detectors shrinks sky areas from long arcs to tens of square degrees.

sections.title: Exercises and further reading
sections.summary: Twenty-one exercises fill in the chapter's omitted algebra: linearized curvature and its Lagrangian, gauge transformations, the Newtonian limit metric, plane-wave Riemann components and canonical form, the 45-degree rotation, the radial wave equation, the two-body Lagrangian and mass moments, second-order Ricci and the Isaacson tensor, TT projection identities and the general quadrupole luminosity via angular averages, geodesic deviation for both polarizations, the spring detector, and oblique-incidence timing. Further reading points to Carroll, Hartle, Schutz, MTW, Andersson's gravitational-wave astronomy text and Synge's five-point curvature detector.
key_moves: Exercises 21.16-21.18 turn the binary-specific luminosity into the general reduced-quadrupole law using the projector and isotropic angular integrals.
Exercise 21.5 connects the Lorentz-gauge equations back to the Newtonian potential and the isotropic Schwarzschild metric.

concepts.name: linearized gravity
concepts.definition: An approximation to general relativity in which the metric is Minkowski plus a small perturbation, g_ab = eta_ab + epsilon h_ab, and all field equations are kept only to first order in epsilon, so that gravity becomes a linear tensor field theory on flat spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by Einstein's original route to gravitational waves; set up in Minkowski coordinates with epsilon as an explicit bookkeeping parameter and a warning that the Lorentz-covariant recasting has limitations, especially for energy.
concepts.notes: Indices on h are raised and lowered with eta because corrections are second order.

concepts.name: asymptotic flatness
concepts.definition: The boundary condition that spacetime approaches Minkowski space far from sources; here imposed as h_ab -> 0 as the radial parameter r -> infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a boundary condition at the start of the linearization; later used to set to zero the integration functions that appear when the plane-wave gauge conditions are integrated.
concepts.notes: Applying this condition to an infinite plane wave, which does not fall off at large r, is logically loose; a novice may notice the tension.

concepts.name: linearized Riemann tensor
concepts.definition: The Riemann tensor of the perturbed metric kept to first order in epsilon: a combination of four second partial derivatives of the perturbation with alternating signs (see formulas), with no products of connection coefficients.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed from the linear Christoffel symbols, which are already first order so products of them drop out.

concepts.name: linearized Ricci and Einstein tensors
concepts.definition: Contractions of the linearized Riemann tensor using eta: the Ricci tensor (epsilon/2)(h^c_a,bc + h^c_b,ac - box h_ab - h_,ab), the scalar epsilon(h^cd_,cd - box h), and the corresponding Einstein tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by contraction immediately after the Riemann tensor; later rewritten via the trace-reversed field, and reused at second order as R^(1)_ab(h^(2)).

concepts.name: d'Alembertian operator
concepts.definition: The flat-spacetime second-order operator box = eta^ab partial_a partial_b, which with signature (+,-,-,-) equals d^2/dt^2 minus the spatial Laplacian.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from the Maxwell chapter when it appears in the linearized Ricci tensor.
concepts.notes: Defined earlier as (12.40).

concepts.name: quadratic Lagrangian for linearized gravity
aliases: Fierz-Pauli Lagrangian (standard name, not used in book)
concepts.definition: A Lagrangian density quadratic in first derivatives of h^ab whose Euler-Lagrange derivative reproduces the linearized Einstein tensor, showing that linearized GR is an ordinary Lagrangian field theory on flat space.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated after the Einstein tensor as an alternative derivation (left as an exercise); later used heuristically to argue that wave energy is quadratic in derivatives of h.

concepts.name: gauge transformation of the metric perturbation
concepts.definition: Under an infinitesimal coordinate change x'^a = x^a + epsilon xi^a, the perturbation changes by h'_ab = h_ab - 2 xi_(a,b) (equivalently - xi_a,b - xi_b,a) while describing the same physical spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the tensor transformation law of the metric and named by analogy with A_a -> A_a + partial_a lambda in electromagnetism.

concepts.name: gauge invariance of linearized curvature
concepts.definition: The linearized Riemann tensor and its contractions are unchanged, to first order, by gauge transformations of h_ab, so curvature (not h itself) is the physical signal of a gravitational field in linearized theory.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted as an easy exercise in §21.2; used in §21.3 to make the propagation argument gauge independent and in §21.11 to prefer geodesic deviation.
prerequisites: gauge transformation of the metric perturbation

concepts.name: trace-reversed perturbation
concepts.definition: The combination phi_ab = h_ab - (1/2) eta_ab h, whose trace is minus that of h; in terms of it the linearized Einstein tensor loses the h_,ab term and becomes a wave operator plus divergence terms. Phi_ab = epsilon phi_ab absorbs the small parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a change of variables that makes the field equations suggestive of wave equations.

concepts.name: Lorentz gauge
concepts.definition: The gauge condition that the trace-reversed perturbation is divergence free, phi^a_b,a = 0 (equivalently h^a_b,a - (1/2) h_,b = 0), under which the linearized Einstein equations become (1/2) epsilon box phi_ab = -kappa T_ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Suggested by looking at which terms in the Einstein tensor prevent a pure wave equation; reachability shown by solving box xi_a = phi^b_a,b for the gauge vector.
prerequisites: gauge transformation of the metric perturbation
concepts.notes: Book calls it the Lorentz gauge; the historically correct EM name is Lorenz.

concepts.name: residual gauge freedom
concepts.definition: Gauge transformations whose generating vector satisfies box xi_a = 0 leave the divergence of phi_ab unchanged, so they can be applied after reaching the Lorentz gauge to simplify the perturbation further.
concepts.how_introduced: Noted immediately after the Lorentz gauge is reached; exploited for plane waves by choosing xi_a as functions of t - x.

concepts.name: linearized field equations as wave equations
concepts.definition: In the Lorentz gauge the linearized Einstein equations read box Phi_ab = -2 kappa T_ab (with kappa = 8 pi in geometric units); in vacuum box phi_ab = 0 and, since the trace also obeys a wave equation, box h_ab = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by inserting the gauge condition into the trace-reversed Einstein tensor; in §21.5 each component is treated as a scalar wave equation with source.

concepts.name: wave equation for the Riemann tensor
aliases: propagation of curvature at light speed
concepts.definition: In linearized vacuum theory in the Lorentz gauge, box R_abcd = 0, so the gauge-invariant curvature itself propagates as a wave at the speed of light.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the better argument for gravitational waves after objecting that h_ab is tied to an arbitrary coordinate system; the authors add that this does not yet show energy transport.
prerequisites: linearized field equations as wave equations
concepts.notes: Energy transport is postponed to §21.8 and Chapter 23.

concepts.name: plane gravitational wave
concepts.definition: A vacuum solution of the linearized equations depending on spacetime only through a single null phase such as u = t - x, representing an infinite planar wavefront moving along x at light speed.
concepts.how_introduced: Built in two steps: first the weaker ansatz h(t, x) to analyse Riemann components, then h(t - x) to integrate the gauge conditions; pictured as parallel planes moving at speed 1.
prerequisites: linearized field equations as wave equations

concepts.name: transverse-traceless gauge
aliases: canonical form of a plane wave
concepts.definition: A gauge for vacuum waves in which h_0a = 0, the spatial part is divergence free and traceless; for a wave along x only h22 = -h33 and h23 are nonzero.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached constructively for a plane wave by integrating Lorentz gauge conditions and using residual gauge vectors; later defined by its conditions in §21.8 and used throughout detection calculations.

concepts.name: two radiative degrees of freedom
concepts.definition: After gauge freedom is removed, a linearized plane gravitational wave is specified by exactly two free functions of the phase (h22 and h23), so the field has two radiation degrees of freedom.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced in the chapter opening and confirmed when the canonical form contains only h22 and h23.

concepts.name: proper distance in a gravitational-wave spacetime
concepts.definition: The invariant spatial length between neighbouring free particles at fixed time in TT coordinates, which for an h22-wave is scaled by (1 - epsilon h22)^(1/2) along one transverse axis and (1 + epsilon h22)^(1/2) along the other.
concepts.how_introduced: Read directly off the line element for neighbouring particles, then integrated over a finite separation in §21.11.

concepts.name: plus polarization
concepts.definition: The polarization state with h22 = -h33 nonzero and h23 = 0: a ring of free particles in the transverse plane is squeezed along one transverse axis while being stretched along the perpendicular one, alternating as the wave oscillates.
concepts.how_introduced: Worked out from proper separations along y and z in the h22 line element, then shown as a time sequence of ring deformations.
prerequisites: proper distance in a gravitational-wave spacetime

concepts.name: cross polarization
concepts.definition: The polarization state with only the off-diagonal h23 nonzero; it produces the same squeeze-stretch pattern as the plus polarization but along axes rotated by 45 degrees in the transverse plane.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by rotating the transverse coordinates by 45 degrees so that the h23 line element takes the h22 form.

concepts.name: transverse nature of gravitational waves
concepts.definition: A linearized gravitational wave changes proper separations only in the plane perpendicular to its propagation direction; separations along the propagation direction are unaffected.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown by checking that particles separated along x keep dsigma^2 = dx^2 in the h22 wave.

concepts.name: tensor versus vector polarization
concepts.definition: The two independent polarizations of a rank-2 symmetric tensor wave are related by a 45-degree rotation, whereas those of a vector (electromagnetic) wave are related by 90 degrees; in general a spin-s field's pattern repeats under rotation by 360/s degrees.
concepts.how_introduced: Remarked after the x polarization is found, with the difference attributed to h_ab being a symmetric tensor and A_a a vector.
concepts.notes: The spin-s generalization is standard physics, not stated in the book.

concepts.name: Dirac delta function
concepts.definition: A distribution concentrated at a point with unit integral, whose integral against any function returns that function's value at the point.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced informally to represent a point source in the wave equation, then used as the sifting tool for superposition and for point-mass densities of binary stars.

concepts.name: fundamental solution of the wave equation
concepts.definition: The causal solution of the wave equation with a spacetime delta source, delta(t - |x|)/(4 pi |x|), a spherical shell of disturbance expanding at light speed with amplitude falling as 1/r; superposing shifted copies solves the equation for any source.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by solving the spherically symmetric point-source problem, fixing the normalization by a ball integral, and then choosing the source strength q(t) to be a delta function.

concepts.name: outgoing-wave (causal) boundary condition
concepts.definition: The choice to keep only the outgoing part u(t - r)/r of the general spherical solution and discard the incoming v(t + r)/r, so that the field is caused by the source's past motion.
concepts.how_introduced: Made explicitly after d'Alembert's solution splits the radial wave into outgoing and incoming parts.
prerequisites: fundamental solution of the wave equation

concepts.name: retarded solution
concepts.definition: The solution of box phi = f given by (1/4 pi) times the integral of f evaluated at the retarded time t - |x - y| divided by |x - y|: each source element contributes what it was doing when a light signal would have left it.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by superposing fundamental solutions over all source points and integrating out the time delta; identified with the Green's-function result from PDE theory.
prerequisites: fundamental solution of the wave equation
formulas: \phi(t,\mathbf x)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{f(t-|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|,\mathbf y)}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|}d^3y

concepts.name: far-zone approximation
concepts.definition: For an observer much farther from a compact source than the source's size R_0, the distance |x - y| from each source point is replaced by the distance r to the source centre in the 1/|x - y| factor.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied to the oscillating-source retarded integral as the first of two simplifications.

concepts.name: long-wavelength approximation
concepts.definition: The assumption that the emitted wavelength is much larger than the source size, so retardation differences across the source are negligible and every source element can be evaluated at the same retarded time t - r.
concepts.how_introduced: Named when the phase omega |x - y| is replaced by omega r for a sinusoidal source; then argued to hold for any compact, slowly varying source.
concepts.notes: Equivalent to requiring internal source velocities much smaller than c.

concepts.name: linearized energy-momentum conservation
concepts.definition: To first order about flat space the covariant conservation law reduces to the ordinary divergence partial_a T^ab = 0, giving continuity of energy and of momentum densities.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken from the Bianchi-identity consequence of Einstein's equations and linearized, as the starting point of the quadrupole derivation; later qualified for self-gravitating binaries.

concepts.name: tensor virial identity
concepts.definition: For a compact source obeying partial_a T^ab = 0, the spatial integral of T^ij equals one half the second time derivative of the integral of x^i x^j T^00.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by differentiating the energy continuity equation in time, using momentum conservation to get a double divergence, and integrating by parts twice against x^l x^m.
concepts.notes: Name 'tensor virial theorem' is standard but not used in the book.

concepts.name: second mass moment
concepts.definition: I^ij(t) = integral of y^i y^j mu(t, y) over space, where mu = T^00 is the mass-energy density; the source quantity whose second time derivative sets the far field.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined right after the tensor virial identity to compress the result into the quadrupole formula; evaluated for two point masses in §21.7.

concepts.name: quadrupole formula for the wave field
concepts.definition: Far from a compact, slowly moving source, the spatial trace-reversed perturbation is Phi_ij(t, x) = -(2/r) times the second time derivative of I_ij evaluated at retarded time t - r (G = c = 1).
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by inserting the tensor virial identity into the long-wavelength far-zone solution.
concepts.notes: Only the TT part of this field is radiative; the book extracts it in §21.9.

concepts.name: reduced-mass two-body problem
concepts.definition: Rewriting two gravitating bodies in terms of centre of mass and relative position, so the centre of mass moves freely and the relative motion is that of a single particle of reduced mass m1 m2/(m1 + m2) in the inverse-square potential.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to set up the Newtonian binary source via its Lagrangian.

concepts.name: Kepler's third law for a circular binary
concepts.definition: For two equal masses m on a circular orbit of separation a = 2R about their centre of mass, Omega^2 = 2Gm/a^3 = Gm/(4R^3).
concepts.how_introduced: From the radial Euler-Lagrange equation with constant angular velocity.

concepts.name: frequency doubling of binary gravitational waves
concepts.definition: A binary on a circular orbit emits quadrupole gravitational waves at twice its orbital angular frequency, because the mass distribution returns to the same configuration after half an orbit.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the double-angle terms in the binary's mass moments; used again when interpreting GW150914's 75 Hz orbital frequency.

concepts.name: gravitational-wave amplitude of a binary
concepts.definition: The amplitude of the quadrupole field of an equal-mass circular binary, A = 8 Omega^2 m R^2 / r in geometric units, falling off as 1/r.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off the waveform matrix (21.108).
prerequisites: quadrupole formula for the wave field

concepts.name: non-localizability of gravitational energy
concepts.definition: In general relativity there is no tensorial, pointwise energy density for the gravitational field: the equivalence principle lets all first derivatives of the metric vanish at any chosen point, and there is no fixed background symmetry to define conserved energy locally, so gravitational energy must be defined globally, quasi-locally or by averaging.
concepts.how_introduced: Given two reasons (equivalence principle and absent background symmetries) with analogies to Newtonian and Maxwell field energy that are quadratic in field gradients.
concepts.notes: Forward pointer to global mass definitions in Chapter 23.

concepts.name: second-order perturbation theory
concepts.definition: Expanding g_ab = eta_ab + epsilon h^(1)_ab + epsilon^2 h^(2)_ab and solving Einstein's equations order by order; at second order the linear operator acting on h^(2) is sourced by terms quadratic in h^(1).
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the systematic way to calculate gravitational-wave energy, with the quadratic Ricci tensor given explicitly (21.114).

concepts.name: effective energy-momentum tensor of gravitational waves
concepts.definition: The tensor t_ab = -(1/8 pi)[R^(2)_ab(h^(1)) - (1/2) eta_ab eta^cd R^(2)_cd(h^(1))], which acts as the source of the second-order metric in the same way matter stress-energy sources the first-order metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by moving the quadratic Ricci terms to the right-hand side of the second-order equation and writing the left side in Einstein-tensor form.
concepts.notes: Not gauge invariant pointwise; the book flags this and the background-split issue.

concepts.name: spacetime averaging
concepts.definition: Replacing a quantity by its mean over a spacetime region several wavelengths across centred on a point; under the average, total derivatives integrate to negligible boundary terms, so derivatives can be moved from one factor to another with a sign change.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to cure the gauge dependence of t_ab and described as making it a quasi-local quantity.
prerequisites: effective energy-momentum tensor of gravitational waves

concepts.name: Isaacson energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: The spacetime average, over a region several wavelengths across, of the effective second-order stress tensor of a gravitational wave. It is a quadratic expression in first derivatives of the perturbation with prefactor 1/32 pi, it is gauge invariant, and in TT gauge only the term contracting the two gradient factors survives.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by averaging (21.117) with integration by parts; gauge invariance asserted after a long calculation; then evaluated for monochromatic waves.

concepts.name: gravitational-wave energy flux
concepts.definition: The averaged energy per unit area per unit time carried by a monochromatic plane wave, (A_+^2 + A_x^2) omega^2 / 32 pi in geometric units, with amplitudes measured in TT gauge; energy density takes the same value.
concepts.how_introduced: First estimated from the quadratic Lagrangian and the one-half average of cos^2, then confirmed from the Isaacson tensor.
concepts.notes: In SI units multiply by c^3/G.

concepts.name: transverse-traceless projection
concepts.definition: For propagation direction n, X^TT_ij = (P_i^k P_j^l - (1/2) P_ij P^kl) X_kl with P_ij = delta_ij - n_i n_j; it keeps the part of a symmetric tensor transverse to n and removes its trace, giving the radiative part.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in §21.9 as a recipe (project transverse, subtract half the trace) after rotating the binary field; formalized in Exercises 21.16-21.17.

concepts.name: angular distribution of binary gravitational radiation
concepts.definition: For a circular binary viewed at angle theta from the orbital axis, A_+ is proportional to (1 + cos^2 theta) and A_x to 2 cos theta, so power per solid angle is proportional to cos^4 theta + 6 cos^2 theta + 1: strongest (both polarizations, circular) along the axis and weakest (pure +, linear) in the orbital plane.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed by rotating the binary field into a frame aligned with the viewing direction and TT-projecting.
concepts.notes: The on-axis/in-plane circular versus linear polarization reading is ours, implied by the amplitudes.

concepts.name: gravitational-wave luminosity
concepts.definition: Total power carried away by gravitational waves, obtained by integrating flux times r^2 over all solid angles; for an equal-mass circular binary it is 128/5 m^2 R^4 Omega^6 (G = c = 1).
concepts.how_introduced: Integral over the sphere of the binary's angular pattern, then re-expressed through the orbital period.
prerequisites: angular distribution of binary gravitational radiation

concepts.name: reduced quadrupole tensor
concepts.definition: The trace-free part of the second mass moment, I-bar_ij = I_ij - (1/3) delta_ij I^k_k.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined when the general luminosity formula is quoted, and evaluated for the binary as a check.
concepts.notes: Printed with a struck-through I.

concepts.name: quadrupole luminosity formula
concepts.definition: The power radiated by a slowly moving compact source is one fifth of the averaged square of the third time derivative of its reduced quadrupole tensor (G = c = 1).
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as the result of a more general calculation (Exercises 21.17-21.18) and verified on the binary.
concepts.notes: In SI units the prefactor is G/(5c^5).

concepts.name: binding energy of a circular binary
concepts.definition: Kinetic plus gravitational potential energy of the equal-mass circular binary, E = -m^2/(4R) = -(m/4)(4 pi m/T)^(2/3) in G = 1 units; it is negative, and becomes more negative as the orbit shrinks.
concepts.how_introduced: Written at the start of §21.10 as the reservoir that radiation drains.
prerequisites: Kepler's third law for a circular binary

concepts.name: orbital decay by gravitational radiation
concepts.definition: Loss of orbital energy to gravitational waves makes a binary's separation and period shrink, with |dT/dt| proportional to T^(-5/3) for a circular orbit, eventually leading to merger.
concepts.how_introduced: Energy balance between the binary's Newtonian energy and the radiated luminosity; tested with binary pulsars.
prerequisites: binding energy of a circular binary
concepts.notes: The book prints dT/dt without the minus sign and says the period increases; physically T decreases.

concepts.name: Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar
concepts.definition: A 59 ms radio pulsar in a 7.75 hour orbit with another neutron star (each about 1.4 solar masses), discovered in 1974, whose orbital period decay matches the general-relativistic gravitational-radiation prediction.
concepts.how_introduced: Narrated after the period-decay formula, with a reproduced plot of cumulative periastron shift.
concepts.notes: Real orbit is highly eccentric (e about 0.62), which boosts the loss rate relative to the circular formula; the book does not mention this.

concepts.name: double pulsar
concepts.definition: A binary of two detected pulsars discovered in 2003 whose periastron-time shift tracks the quadrupole-emission prediction closely.
concepts.how_introduced: Second observational confirmation, with plot.
concepts.notes: The book writes J0737-3029; the standard designation is J0737-3039.

concepts.name: geodesic motion of test masses in a gravitational wave
concepts.definition: A test particle initially at rest in TT coordinates stays at fixed spatial coordinates while a wave passes, because the first-order geodesic equation involves only Gamma^a_00, which vanishes in TT gauge.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by perturbing the rest 4-velocity and linearizing the geodesic equation.

concepts.name: TT coordinates as comoving coordinates
aliases: TT gauge comoving with free particles
concepts.definition: Because free particles keep fixed TT coordinates and g_00 = 1, g_0i = 0, TT coordinates are carried along with freely falling test masses and TT time equals their proper time; physical effects show up only in proper distances and light travel times.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn as a consequence of the geodesic calculation and used to simplify the radar computation.
prerequisites: geodesic motion of test masses in a gravitational wave

concepts.name: geodesic deviation
concepts.definition: The relative acceleration of neighbouring free particles is given by the Riemann tensor acting on their separation, D^2 eta^alpha / D tau^2 = -R^alpha_0beta0 eta^beta in an adapted tetrad; for a wave it yields oscillating transverse strains.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from Chapter 10 as a gauge-invariant check of the proper-distance result, with plane-wave Riemann components inserted.

concepts.name: resonant bar detector
concepts.definition: A massive elastic body (bar or sphere), isolated and cooled, whose fundamental mode is driven by the tidal strain of a gravitational wave near its resonant frequency.
concepts.how_introduced: Historical account of Weber's 1960s claims, then a two-masses-on-a-spring model driven by the wave; later assessed in the detector survey.

concepts.name: driven damped oscillator resonance
concepts.definition: A damped oscillator forced sinusoidally reaches a steady amplitude that peaks when the driving frequency matches its natural frequency, with the peak height inversely proportional to the damping.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied to the spring model of a bar driven by an h22 wave.
concepts.notes: The book's numerical factors in (21.160)-(21.161) are inconsistent with its damping term 2 gamma; see gaps.

concepts.name: laser interferometer detector
concepts.definition: An L-shaped interferometer whose suspended mirrors act as free test masses; a gravitational wave lengthens one arm and shortens the other, and the resulting difference in light travel time changes the interference at the output photodetector.
concepts.how_introduced: Described after the bar, with a schematic including 4 km Fabry-Perot cavities, an arm-length difference calculation, and an order-of-magnitude fringe estimate showing why a plain Michelson would fail.
prerequisites: proper distance in a gravitational-wave spacetime

concepts.name: gravitational-wave strain
aliases: fractional length change Delta L / L
concepts.definition: The dimensionless fractional change in proper separation produced by a wave, of order the metric perturbation amplitude; for Earth-reaching waves it is at most about 10^-21.
concepts.how_introduced: Implicit in the proper-distance and interferometer formulas; quoted numerically in detector sensitivities.
prerequisites: proper distance in a gravitational-wave spacetime

concepts.name: radar ranging in curved spacetime
concepts.definition: Measuring distance by timing a light pulse's round trip with a freely falling observer's clock and taking half the elapsed proper time; enough such measurements determine the spacetime geometry (Synge's term: differential chronometry).
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the curved-spacetime extension of the Chapter 2 k-calculus, motivated by the failure of the proper-distance shortcut for large detectors.

concepts.name: round-trip light travel time in a gravitational wave
concepts.definition: The coordinate (and proper) time for a photon to go from a free mass to another at TT coordinate distance L and back; to first order it is 2L minus epsilon/2 times the integrals of h22 sampled along the outgoing and returning flat light paths.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed by integrating the null condition along each leg with the unperturbed straight ray substituted inside h22.

concepts.name: detector response beyond the long-wavelength limit
concepts.definition: When arm length is comparable to or larger than the gravitational wavelength, the wave changes appreciably during the light's transit, so the response depends on the wave at several times (emission, reflection, return) and on incidence angle rather than on a single instantaneous strain.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by LISA and pulsar timing, derived via the exact first-order timing formula, and generalized to oblique incidence in (21.179).
prerequisites: round-trip light travel time in a gravitational wave

concepts.name: LISA
concepts.definition: A planned space-based interferometer of three drag-free spacecraft in a 2.5 million km triangle trailing Earth around the Sun, sensitive to millihertz gravitational waves from sources such as massive black-hole binaries, extreme-mass-ratio inspirals and galactic white-dwarf binaries.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the escape from ground seismic noise below a few hertz, with a figure of its orbital configuration.
prerequisites: detector response beyond the long-wavelength limit
concepts.notes: Book: selected by ESA 2017, launch aimed at 2034. ESA formally adopted the mission in January 2024 with launch planned around 2035 (outside the book).

concepts.name: Doppler tracking
concepts.definition: Monitoring the round-trip radio link to a distant spacecraft for timing fluctuations; a gravitational-wave burst shorter than the round trip appears three times (at transmitter, spacecraft, receiver).
concepts.how_introduced: Listed among detector types as a practical use of the timing formula.
prerequisites: round-trip light travel time in a gravitational wave

concepts.name: pulsar timing array
concepts.definition: A set of millisecond pulsars timed over years; a gravitational wave shifts arrival times through a pulsar term and an Earth term, and the Earth term is correlated between pulsars, allowing detection of nanohertz waves.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed as the fourth detector type, with Parkes, European and NANOGrav arrays named.
prerequisites: round-trip light travel time in a gravitational wave
concepts.notes: In 2023 several PTA collaborations reported evidence for a nanohertz stochastic background (after the book).

concepts.name: burst, periodic and stochastic sources
concepts.definition: A classification of gravitational-wave sources by time structure: short bursts (mergers, captures), long-lived periodic signals (binaries far from merger, spinning neutron stars), and stochastic backgrounds (primordial or unresolved populations).
concepts.how_introduced: Attributed to Thorne at the start of the sources section, with example systems in each class.

concepts.name: numerical relativity
concepts.definition: Solving the full Einstein equations on computers to model strong-field dynamics such as black-hole mergers and stellar collapse, where perturbative methods fail.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as necessary for source estimates and for merger-phase waveform templates.

concepts.name: characteristic strain
concepts.definition: A measure of signal strength that includes the accumulation of signal over the observing time (roughly strain times the square root of the number of cycles observed), used on sensitivity plots instead of the instantaneous strain.
concepts.how_introduced: Clarified when explaining the vertical axis of the source-strength plot.
concepts.notes: The 'number of cycles' description is ours.

concepts.name: matched filtering
concepts.definition: Cross-correlating detector data against a bank of theoretical waveforms spanning source parameters; a genuine signal gives a strong match in each detector within the allowed light-travel delay, and the best template gives the source's parameters.
concepts.how_introduced: Explained in the context of confirming GW150914 and extracting masses and distance.

concepts.name: chirp waveform
concepts.definition: The characteristic signal of a coalescing compact binary: oscillations whose frequency and amplitude rise as the orbit shrinks, peaking at merger and then decaying in a ringdown.
concepts.how_introduced: Described for GW150914 and seen in the reproduced strain data.
prerequisites: frequency doubling of binary gravitational waves

concepts.name: GW150914
aliases: first direct detection of gravitational waves
concepts.definition: The binary black-hole merger signal recorded by both Advanced LIGO detectors on 14 September 2015: about 35 + 30 solar masses forming a roughly 62 solar-mass spinning black hole about 1.4 billion light years away, with about 3 solar masses radiated.
concepts.how_introduced: Narrated with the detection history, figure of the two-site strain data, and parameters extracted by matched filtering.

concepts.name: sky localization by a detector network
concepts.definition: Inferring a source's sky position from differences in arrival times (and amplitudes) at several widely separated detectors; two detectors give a ring or arc, three or more shrink the region to tens of square degrees.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with optical telescopes' narrow fields; illustrated with GW150914 (two detectors) and GW170814 (three).

concepts.name: multi-messenger astronomy
concepts.definition: Observing the same astrophysical event through different carriers (gravitational waves, light across the spectrum, neutrinos); first achieved for gravitational waves with the binary neutron-star merger GW170817.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned at the end of the event summary.
prerequisites: sky localization by a detector network

concepts.name: quasinormal-mode ringdown
aliases: quasi-normal modes of the Kerr solution
concepts.definition: The damped oscillations with which a perturbed black hole settles to a stationary Kerr state; their frequencies and damping times depend only on the final mass and spin.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the model for the final phase of merger templates.

concepts.name: post-Newtonian approximation
concepts.definition: A systematic expansion of general relativity in powers of v/c (equivalently GM/rc^2) about Newtonian dynamics, used to model the inspiral of compact binaries.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the method for early-inspiral templates, with a pointer to Blanchet's review.

key_equations.name: Weak-field metric
key_equations.meaning: Spacetime metric as flat Minkowski plus a small perturbation; all later results are first order in epsilon.
key_equations.symbols: eta_ab Minkowski metric in Minkowski coordinates; epsilon small dimensionless bookkeeping parameter; h_ab perturbation

key_equations.name: Asymptotic flatness
key_equations.meaning: Perturbation vanishes far away; later kills integration functions in the plane-wave reduction.
key_equations.symbols: r radial parameter

key_equations.name: Inverse metric
key_equations.meaning: First-order inverse; indices on h are raised with eta.

key_equations.name: Linearized Christoffel symbols
key_equations.meaning: Connection is first order in epsilon, so products of Christoffel symbols drop out of curvature.
key_equations.symbols: comma denotes partial derivative

key_equations.name: Linearized Riemann tensor
key_equations.meaning: Curvature of the perturbed metric to first order; gauge invariant.

key_equations.name: Bianchi identities, linearized
key_equations.meaning: At first order the covariant derivative in the Bianchi identity becomes a partial derivative, and (21.7) satisfies it identically.
key_equations.symbols: square brackets denote antisymmetrization

key_equations.name: Linearized Ricci tensor
key_equations.meaning: Ricci tensor in terms of h and its trace; reused at second order as R^(1)_ab.
key_equations.symbols: h = eta^cd h_cd (21.11); Box = eta^ab d_a d_b = d_t^2 - nabla^2

key_equations.name: Linearized Ricci scalar
key_equations.meaning: Trace of the linear Ricci tensor.

key_equations.name: Linearized Einstein tensor
key_equations.meaning: Left-hand side of the linearized field equations.

key_equations.name: Lagrangian for linearized gravity
key_equations.meaning: Linear Einstein tensor is the Euler-Lagrange derivative of a Lagrangian quadratic in first derivatives of h.
key_equations.symbols: trace indices on the h^c_{,a} terms reconstructed from context (OCR shows h^c_{,a})

key_equations.name: Gauge transformation
key_equations.meaning: Infinitesimal coordinate changes shift the perturbation by a symmetrized gradient without changing physics.
key_equations.symbols: xi^a gauge vector; round brackets symmetrize

key_equations.name: Trace-reversed perturbation
key_equations.meaning: Variable that makes the Einstein tensor a wave operator plus divergences.

key_equations.name: Einstein tensor via phi
key_equations.meaning: Divergence terms vanish in the Lorentz gauge.

key_equations.name: Lorentz gauge condition
key_equations.meaning: Divergence-free trace-reversed field; also called de Donder or harmonic gauge.

key_equations.name: Reaching the Lorentz gauge
key_equations.meaning: The gauge is reached by solving a sourced wave equation for the gauge vector.

key_equations.name: Linearized field equations in Lorentz gauge
key_equations.meaning: Gravity in the weak field obeys a wave equation sourced by stress-energy.
key_equations.symbols: kappa Einstein coupling (8 pi in geometric units)

key_equations.name: Residual gauge condition
key_equations.meaning: Gauge vectors obeying the homogeneous wave equation preserve the Lorentz gauge.

key_equations.name: Vacuum wave equations
key_equations.meaning: In vacuum and Lorentz gauge both the trace-reversed and the original perturbation obey the wave equation.

key_equations.name: Wave equation for curvature
key_equations.meaning: Gauge-invariant evidence that gravitational disturbances propagate at light speed.

key_equations.name: Plane-symmetric ansatz
key_equations.meaning: Perturbation independent of the transverse coordinates.
key_equations.symbols: coordinate index 0 is time; indices 1, 2, 3 are the Cartesian axes, with 1 the propagation direction

key_equations.name: Riemann components of a plane wave
key_equations.meaning: Three groups: identically zero, a mixed group killed by the vacuum equations, and a group built only from h22, h23, h33.
key_equations.symbols: full lists in the book: six zero components, five in (21.39), nine in (21.40)

key_equations.name: Plane wave along x
key_equations.meaning: Wave travelling in +x at light speed.

key_equations.name: Integrated gauge conditions
key_equations.meaning: Lorentz gauge plus boundary conditions tie components together, leaving h00, h11, h02, h03, h22, h23.

key_equations.name: Residual gauge functions
key_equations.meaning: Gauge vector xi_a = F_a(t - x) automatically satisfies Box xi = 0 and removes h00, h11, h02, h03.

key_equations.name: Canonical (TT) plane wave
key_equations.meaning: A plane wave has only two physical functions, h22(t - x) and h23(t - x): transverse and traceless.

key_equations.name: Line element of + wave
key_equations.meaning: Transverse axes are scaled in opposite senses.

key_equations.name: Proper separations in + wave
key_equations.meaning: Positive h22 brings y-neighbours closer and pushes z-neighbours apart.
key_equations.symbols: d sigma^2 = -ds^2 at fixed t

key_equations.name: x wave and 45-degree rotation
key_equations.latex: ds^2=dt^2-dx^2-dy^2+2\varepsilon h_{23}dy\,dz-dz^2\;\xrightarrow{\bar y=(y+z)/\sqrt2,\ \bar z=(-y+z)/\sqrt2}\;dt^2-dx^2-[1-\varepsilon h_{23}]d\bar y^2-[1+\varepsilon h_{23}]d\bar z^2
key_equations.meaning: The cross polarization is the plus polarization on axes rotated by 45 degrees.

key_equations.name: Sourced wave equation
key_equations.meaning: Field equation to be solved for radiation from sources.

key_equations.name: Point-source wave equation
key_equations.meaning: Building-block problem with a time-varying source at the origin.
key_equations.symbols: q(t) source strength

key_equations.name: Radial reduction and outgoing solution
key_equations.meaning: Away from the source r phi obeys the 1D wave equation; causality keeps only the outgoing part.

key_equations.name: Normalization and fundamental solution
key_equations.meaning: Ball integration fixes the amplitude; a delta-in-time source gives the retarded Green's function.

key_equations.name: Retarded solution
key_equations.latex: \phi(t,\mathbf x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(t-|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|,\mathbf y)}{|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|}d^3y
key_equations.meaning: General causal solution of the sourced wave equation.
key_equations.symbols: f source term

key_equations.name: Far-zone and long-wavelength conditions
key_equations.meaning: Observer far away and source small compared with the emitted wavelength.
key_equations.symbols: R_0 source radius

key_equations.name: Far-zone long-wavelength solution
key_equations.meaning: Whole source evaluated at one retarded time.

key_equations.name: Far field of a compact source
key_equations.latex: \Phi_{ab}(t,\mathbf x)=-\frac{2\kappa}{4\pi r}\int T_{ab}(t-r,\mathbf y)d^3y=-\frac4r\int T_{ab}(t-r,\mathbf y)d^3y
key_equations.meaning: Geometric units, kappa = 8 pi.

key_equations.name: Double divergence from conservation
key_equations.meaning: Energy and momentum conservation link the density's acceleration to stresses.
key_equations.symbols: i, j, k run over 1..3

key_equations.name: Tensor virial identity
key_equations.meaning: Stress integral equals half the second time derivative of the mass moment for a compact source.

key_equations.name: Far field in terms of the mass-energy density
key_equations.meaning: Intermediate form obtained by substituting the stress-integral identity into the far-zone solution; naming the integral I^ij then gives the quadrupole formula.
key_equations.symbols: T^00 = mass-energy density mu; indices moved with delta_ij

key_equations.name: Second mass moment
key_equations.meaning: Source quantity controlling quadrupole emission.
key_equations.symbols: mu = T^00 mass-energy density

key_equations.name: Quadrupole formula (field)
key_equations.meaning: Far-zone wave field is set by the second time derivative of the mass moment at retarded time.
key_equations.symbols: indices lowered with delta_ij; overdot d/dt

key_equations.name: Two-body Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: Relative motion is a single reduced-mass particle in an inverse-square field (centre of mass at rest at origin).
key_equations.symbols: note: book's (21.100) prints the centre-of-mass kinetic term with the relative velocity; it should involve the centre-of-mass velocity

key_equations.name: Kepler relation for equal-mass circular binary
key_equations.meaning: Orbital radius and angular frequency relation.
key_equations.symbols: m each mass; R radius of each star's circle

key_equations.name: Point-mass density of binary
key_equations.meaning: Two equal stars on opposite sides of a circle in the xy-plane.
key_equations.symbols: equation garbled in the page export; recovered from the rendered page

key_equations.name: Binary mass moments
key_equations.latex: I_{xx}=mR^2(1+\cos2\Omega t),\ I_{yy}=mR^2(1-\cos2\Omega t),\ I_{xy}=mR^2\sin2\Omega t
key_equations.meaning: Oscillating parts at twice the orbital frequency; other components zero.

key_equations.name: Binary waveform
key_equations.meaning: Quadrupole radiation of a circular equal-mass binary; transverse-traceless with respect to the orbital axis.

key_equations.name: Frequency and amplitude
key_equations.meaning: Wave frequency is twice orbital; amplitude falls as 1/r.

key_equations.name: Time-averaged energy flux
key_equations.meaning: Energy per unit area per unit time for a monochromatic wave, amplitudes measured in TT gauge.

key_equations.name: Quadratic Ricci tensor
key_equations.meaning: Part of the Ricci tensor quadratic in the first-order perturbation.

key_equations.name: Second-order equation and effective stress tensor
key_equations.meaning: Quadratic terms of the first-order wave act as stress-energy sourcing the second-order metric.

key_equations.name: Spacetime average and integration by parts
key_equations.meaning: Moving average over several wavelengths; total derivatives average to zero.

key_equations.name: Isaacson energy-momentum tensor
key_equations.meaning: Gauge-invariant averaged stress-energy of gravitational waves.

key_equations.name: Gauge invariance of the average
key_equations.meaning: Averaging removes the gauge dependence of the pointwise tensor.

key_equations.name: Isaacson tensor in TT gauge
key_equations.meaning: Only one term survives when h is TT and obeys the vacuum wave equation.

key_equations.name: Energy density of x wave
key_equations.meaning: C_hl C^hl = 2 h_x^2, and the cos^2 average is one half.

key_equations.name: Energy density and flux, both polarizations
key_equations.meaning: Energy density equals flux for a wave moving at light speed; agrees with (21.113).

key_equations.name: Luminosity per solid angle from flux
key_equations.meaning: Power into a small solid angle is the flux times r^2; the 1/r fall-off of the amplitude cancels the r^2, so the result is independent of distance.
key_equations.symbols: dS = solid-angle element; A = TT amplitude of one polarization

key_equations.name: On-axis luminosity per solid angle
key_equations.meaning: Both polarizations contribute equally along the orbital axis.
key_equations.symbols: dS element of solid angle

key_equations.name: Rotation to viewing direction
key_equations.meaning: Express the binary field in a frame whose third axis is the direction at angle theta.

key_equations.name: Polarization amplitudes vs inclination
key_equations.meaning: After TT projection the + amplitude depends on 1 + cos^2 theta and the x amplitude on cos theta.
key_equations.symbols: theta angle from the orbital axis

key_equations.name: Angular radiation pattern
key_equations.meaning: Power per solid angle in direction theta.

key_equations.name: Binary luminosity
key_equations.meaning: Total power radiated by an equal-mass circular binary (G = c = 1).
key_equations.symbols: T orbital period

key_equations.name: Quadrupole luminosity formula
key_equations.meaning: General power formula in terms of the reduced (trace-free) quadrupole.
key_equations.symbols: bar I printed as struck-through I; triple overdot third time derivative

key_equations.name: Reduced quadrupole check for the binary
key_equations.latex: \bar I_{ij}=mR^2\begin{pmatrix}\cos2\Omega t+\frac13&\sin2\Omega t&0\\ \sin2\Omega t&-\cos2\Omega t+\frac13&0\\0&0&-\frac23\end{pmatrix},\ \dddot{\bar I}_{ij}\dddot{\bar I}{}^{ij}=128m^2R^4\Omega^6
key_equations.meaning: The general formula reproduces the angular-integration result 128/5.
